stem:
Mukanya Garments is a fictional clothing manufacturer in Bulawayo. In 2025 the owner, Mrs Mukanya, cut the annual training programme to save US\$20,000, froze pay for the year and stopped the monthly meetings between managers and workers. Workers complained that managers no longer listened. A union representative has asked for a workers' committee. The owner says that "workers only work for money". The table shows figures for the last two years.

|  | 2024 | 2025 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Employees at 1 January | 96 | 104 |
| Employees at 31 December | 104 | 100 |
| Employees who left during the year | 12 | 25 |
| Garments produced | 41,000 | 40,800 |
| Working days available | 24,000 | 24,480 |
| Working days lost to absence | 1,920 | 2,448 |
| Wage bill (US\$) | 380,000 | 365,000 |

The factory has 24,000 working days available in 2024 and 24,480 in 2025 because of the change in numbers. Labour turnover = employees leaving ÷ average number of employees × 100. Absence rate = working days lost to absence ÷ working days available × 100.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: From the table, state:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the number of employees who left in 2025;
parts.explanation: The table shows 25 leavers in 2025.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the number of garments produced in 2024.
parts.explanation: The table shows 41,000 garments in 2024.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the labour turnover, to one decimal place, for:

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate, for the factory:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: output per worker in 2025 (use the average number of employees);
parts.explanation: Output per worker = 40,800 ÷ 102 = 400 garments.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the percentage fall in output per worker from 2024 (410) to 2025, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Analyse how the decisions taken by Mrs Mukanya in 2025 may have led to the change in labour turnover.

points.description: Labour turnover rose from 12.0% to 24.5% after the changes
Ending training means workers have no chance to develop skills or prospects, so they may look for jobs elsewhere
Application: the US\$20,000 saved on training is small compared with the cost of replacing 25 leavers
A pay freeze means workers may find better-paid jobs elsewhere
Stopping meetings reduced communication, so workers felt unvalued and morale fell

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Labour turnover rose from 12.0% to 24.5% after Mrs Mukanya's changes. Ending training gave workers no chance to develop skills or prospects, and a pay freeze meant that rival firms could offer more, so some looked for work elsewhere. Stopping the meetings reduced communication, so workers felt that managers did not value them and their morale fell. The US\$20,000 saved on training is small compared with the cost of replacing 25 leavers.

parts.explanation: Each decision is linked to a cause of leaving and to cost.
hints: Link each decision to a reason for leaving.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain two non-financial methods that Mrs Mukanya could use to motivate her workers.

points.description: Restore consultation through a workers' committee or regular meetings
Application: workers would feel listened to and could raise their complaints
Offer training and promotion opportunities
Application: the training programme could be reintroduced, giving workers prospects

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: She could set up a workers' committee and restore the monthly meetings, so that workers feel listened to and can raise their complaints. She could also bring back the training programme and offer promotion, which would give workers prospects and a reason to stay.

parts.explanation: Two methods, each applied.
hints: Use the complaints in the case.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Mrs Mukanya says that "workers only work for money". Discuss this view, and advise her on what to do.

points.description: Money matters: the pay freeze may have contributed to workers leaving
Herzberg: pay is a hygiene factor, so unfair pay causes dissatisfaction but does not alone motivate
Workers' complaints concern communication, which suggests they want to be listened to
Application: output per worker fell 2.4% and absence rose from 8.0% to 10.0%, suggesting poor morale
Money alone costs more, but non-financial changes (meetings, training) cost less
Recommendation with a reason: restore consultation and training and review pay

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Money matters, and the pay freeze may have contributed to workers leaving. But the complaints are about communication, and Herzberg argued that pay is a hygiene factor that prevents dissatisfaction but does not alone motivate. Output per worker fell by 2.4% and absence rose from 8.0% to 10.0%, which suggests poor morale and not only pay. She should restore the meetings and the training, which cost less than a general pay rise, and review pay if turnover stays high.

parts.explanation: Weighs money against other motivators with evidence and gives advice.
hints: Use the complaints, the absence rates and Herzberg.

explanation: Turnover 12.0% and 24.5%; output per worker 400 (a fall of 2.4%); the cuts raised turnover and lowered morale.
hints: Use the average number of employees.
Output per worker = garments ÷ average employees.

stem: Essay. Motivated workers produce more and stay longer in a business.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe four financial methods that a business can use to motivate its employees. [10 marks]

points.description: Piece rate: pay for each unit produced
Development: rewards effort but quality may fall
Commission: a percentage of the value of sales
Development: suits sales staff but may pressure customers
Bonus: a one-off payment for reaching a target
Development: rewards achievement but may be short-term
Profit sharing: a share of profit paid to employees
Development: links pay to the success of the firm but the effect of one worker is small
Link to motivation: pay linked to results gives a reason to work harder
Example from a Zimbabwean business, such as a bakery or garment factory

levels.descriptor: Four methods clearly described and developed, with an example and a link to motivation
Three or four methods described with some development

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A business can pay by results. A piece rate pays a fixed sum for every unit produced, as in a garment factory where sewers are paid for each shirt; it rewards effort, but quality may fall as workers hurry. Commission pays a percentage of the value of sales, which suits sales staff in a hardware shop, although it may lead to pressure on customers. A bonus is a one-off payment for reaching a target, such as delivering an order on time; it rewards achievement but its effect may be short-lived. Profit sharing gives employees a share of the profit, which links their pay to the success of the firm and encourages teamwork, although one worker's effort has little effect on the total. Each method motivates by giving workers a financial reason to work harder, but each has costs and side effects.

parts.explanation: Four methods, each described and developed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss whether financial methods are more effective than non-financial methods in motivating the employees of a Zimbabwean manufacturing firm. [15 marks]

points.description: Financial methods give a clear and immediate reward
Pay is needed to meet workers' basic needs (Maslow: physiological and security needs)
Variable pay links labour cost to output, protecting the firm in a poor year
Application: piece rate in a garment factory raises output
Limit: pay is a hygiene factor (Herzberg); it prevents dissatisfaction but does not alone motivate
Limit: financial methods can reduce quality or damage teamwork
Non-financial methods meet higher needs such as achievement and recognition
Job enrichment and empowerment give responsibility and interest
Team working and participation give a sense of belonging and a voice
Training and promotion show a future in the firm
Application: a workers' committee can reduce conflict at low cost
Limit: non-financial methods are slower, cost training and managers' time, and cannot replace fair pay
Different workers are motivated by different things, so the best method depends on the workers and the job
Judgement: a mix is better than either alone, with fair pay as the basis
Reasoned conclusion linked to the firm, such as piece rate with quality checks plus participation

levels.descriptor: Balanced argument on both types, using theory and the context of a manufacturing firm; a justified, qualified judgement
Both types explained with some application; judgement weakly supported

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Financial methods have clear advantages. Workers must be able to meet their basic needs, so fair pay is essential, and a piece rate or bonus gives an immediate reward for effort. Variable pay also links the firm's labour cost to its output, which protects it in a poor year. However, Herzberg argued that pay is a hygiene factor: unfair pay causes dissatisfaction, but it does not alone create lasting motivation. Financial methods can also cause harm, as a piece rate may cause workers to hurry and spoil goods, and individual bonuses may damage teamwork. Non-financial methods meet higher needs. Job enrichment and empowerment give operators interest and responsibility, team working gives a sense of belonging, and training and promotion show a future. A workers' committee gives a voice at low cost. But they are slower to work, need managers' time and training, and cannot replace fair pay. Different workers want different things: a young operator may want promotion, while a family breadwinner may value a bonus. In a Zimbabwean manufacturing firm, the best approach is a mix: fair basic pay with a piece rate or bonus linked to quality, supported by participation and training. Financial methods are therefore not more effective on their own; they are the base on which non-financial methods build.

parts.explanation: Weighs both kinds using theory and context, ending with a qualified judgement.

explanation: Describe four financial methods; discuss both kinds and conclude that a mix, with fair pay as the base, is best.
hints: Use Herzberg and Maslow in part (b).
Reach a judgement that depends on the workers and the job.

stem: Essay. Managers use analytical tools to plan the future of a business.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain how SWOT analysis and PEST analysis can help the managers of a small business to plan. [10 marks]

points.description: SWOT sorts internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats
Development: strengths such as loyal customers can be matched to opportunities
Weaknesses such as lack of cash show what must be improved before growth
Development: threats such as a new rival show what must be defended against
PEST examines political, economic, social and technological factors outside the business
Development: economic factors such as inflation or interest rates affect costs and demand
Social and technological changes show new customer needs and new methods
Together they help managers to choose a strategy that fits the business and its environment
Application to a small business, such as a bakery or hardware shop
Limitation or condition: the analysis must be kept up to date and turned into action

levels.descriptor: Both tools explained and developed, with application to a small business and a link to planning
Both tools explained with some development
Names parts of the tools with little explanation

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A SWOT analysis sorts what a business knows into internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats. For a small bakery, loyal customers are a strength that can be matched to an opportunity such as demand from small shops, while a weakness such as lack of cash shows that expansion must be financed carefully, and a new supermarket is a threat to be defended against. A PEST analysis examines factors outside the business: political, economic, social and technological. Rising interest rates, for example, raise the cost of loans and may reduce customers' spending, while a change in tastes or a new payment technology may create new opportunities. Used together, the tools help managers to choose a strategy that fits both the business and its surroundings, so long as the analysis is kept up to date and turned into action.

parts.explanation: Both tools explained and applied to planning.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss which growth strategy from the Ansoff matrix a small manufacturer in Zimbabwe should adopt. [15 marks]

points.description: Ansoff has four strategies formed from products and markets, existing or new
Market penetration: more sales of the same product to the same customers; lowest risk
Penetration may offer limited growth if the market is small
Product development: a new product for existing customers; medium risk
It uses the firm's knowledge of its customers but the product may fail
Market development: existing product in a new market; medium risk
It uses the firm's product knowledge but the new market is unfamiliar
Diversification: new product in a new market; highest risk
It spreads risk across products but the firm lacks experience of either
Choice depends on the firm's resources, such as cash and skills
Core competence: the firm should choose the route that uses its strengths
Market conditions: size of the market, competition and growth
Risk attitude of the owner and the cost of failure for a small firm
Judgement: usually penetration or product development first, because they carry less risk
Reasoned conclusion linked to the manufacturer, with a condition

levels.descriptor: All four strategies explained with risk and application; weighs factors affecting the choice; a justified recommendation with a condition
Explains some strategies with some application; judgement weakly supported

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The Ansoff matrix gives four growth strategies. Market penetration sells more of the same product to the same customers; it has the lowest risk because the firm knows both, but growth may be limited if the market is small. Product development offers a new product to existing customers; the firm knows its customers, but the new product may fail. Market development sells the existing product in a new market, such as another province, using the firm's product knowledge, but the new market may be unfamiliar. Diversification is a new product in a new market; it has the highest risk because the firm has no experience of either, although it spreads dependence. The best choice depends on the manufacturer's resources and skills. A small manufacturer with limited cash cannot afford the loss from a failed diversification, so penetration or product development will usually be preferred, building on its core competence. Market development may be sensible if the home market is small and competition is strong. The firm should first use penetration and product development, and move to market development only when it has the cash to survive a slow start.

parts.explanation: Explains all four strategies with their risks and recommends a low-risk route with a condition.

explanation: Explain SWOT and PEST for planning; discuss Ansoff strategies by risk and resources and recommend a low-risk route first.
hints: Explain each Ansoff strategy with its risk before choosing.

stem:
Case study. Dube Brothers Hardware is a fictional chain of building-supply shops in Bulawayo, Gweru and Masvingo. It started 2025 with 150 employees and ended with 170 after opening a new branch. The managing director, Mr Dube, believes that the new branch has stretched management. Workers complain about long hours, rushed induction for new staff and two recent accidents with unguarded cutting equipment. A SWOT analysis completed by the managers lists a good reputation and loyal builders as strengths; weak stock control and low pay for shop assistants as weaknesses; a rise in construction in Masvingo as an opportunity; and a new national chain entering Bulawayo as a threat. Mr Dube must now choose between two plans for 2026: (A) build a distribution warehouse, or (B) improve and extend the existing shops. The table shows some figures.

|  | 2024 | 2025 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Employees at 1 January | 150 | 150 |
| Employees at 31 December | 150 | 170 |
| Employees who left | 18 | 24 |
| Average monthly pay per employee (US\$) | 300 | 300 |
| Revenue (US\$) | 1,480,000 | 1,560,000 |
| Profit for the year (US\$) | 118,000 | 96,000 |
| Market share (%) | 24 | 22 |

Plan A would cost US\$90,000 and bring in US\$260,000 if construction demand stays strong and US\$110,000 if it weakens. Plan B would cost US\$60,000 and bring in US\$190,000 if demand stays strong and US\$120,000 if it weakens (amounts before the cost of the plan). Mr Dube estimates a 0.57 chance that demand stays strong and a 0.43 chance that it weakens.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the labour turnover for 2025, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Employees are paid an average of US\$300 a month. Calculate the increase in the annual wage bill caused by the rise in employees from 150 to 170.
parts.explanation: Annual wage bill 2025 (170 staff) = 170 × 300 × 12 = 612,000. With 150 staff = 540,000. Increase = US\$72,000.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the net expected value of:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Plan A;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Plan B.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Using the SWOT analysis in the case, explain how Mr Dube could use one strength to deal with one threat.

points.description: The strength: a good reputation and loyal builders
The threat: a new national chain entering Bulawayo
Application: loyal builders are less likely to switch, so the shops can protect sales
Mr Dube could build on this by offering credit or delivery to regular builders

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The shops' good reputation and loyal builders are a strength that can be used against the threat of the new national chain in Bulawayo. Loyal builders are less likely to switch, so sales are protected, and Mr Dube could reinforce this by offering regular builders credit or delivery.

parts.explanation: A strength applied to a threat.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Analyse the possible effects on the business of the workers' complaints about long hours, rushed induction and unguarded equipment.

points.description: Long hours cause tiredness and stress, leading to errors and absence
Rushed induction means new staff do not understand the job or safety rules
Application: 20 extra staff joined during the year, so many may be affected
Unguarded equipment caused two accidents, risking injury and legal action
Accidents bring absence, compensation and lost output
Morale falls and labour turnover may rise from 15.0%, increasing recruitment costs

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Long hours cause tiredness and stress, which lead to errors and absence. Rushed induction means that the 20 new staff may not understand the job or the safety rules, which makes accidents more likely. Unguarded equipment has already caused two accidents, which bring injury, absence, compensation and lost output, and may lead to legal action. These problems lower morale, so labour turnover may rise above 15.0%, increasing recruitment and training costs.

parts.explanation: Chains from each complaint to cost.
hints: Connect each complaint to a cost to the business.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Evaluate which plan Mr Dube should choose, and what he should do about the staff problems. Use the figures in the case.

points.description: Plan A has the higher net expected value (US\$105,500 against US\$99,900), a difference of US\$5,600
The difference rests on estimated probabilities and is small
Plan A costs US\$30,000 more and its worst case is lower: 110,000 − 90,000 = US\$20,000 against 120,000 − 60,000 = US\$60,000
Profit fell from US\$118,000 to US\$96,000 and market share fell from 24% to 22%, so the business may not afford a risky plan
Management is stretched and staff problems are not solved, so a large new project may worsen them
Judgement with a reason and condition, for example Plan B first, while fixing safety and induction

levels.descriptor: Uses the figures for both plans and the case evidence about profit, management and staff; weighs risk against return; a justified recommendation with a condition
Applies some figures with some analysis; judgement weakly supported
States figures or features with little analysis

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: On expected value Plan A is better, with a net US\$105,500 against US\$99,900 for Plan B, but the gap of US\$5,600 rests on estimated probabilities. Plan A costs US\$30,000 more and has a much worse worst case: 110,000 − 90,000 = US\$20,000, against US\$60,000 for Plan B. Profit has fallen from US\$118,000 to US\$96,000 and market share from 24% to 22%, so the business can afford little risk, and management is already stretched by the new branch and by the staff problems. Mr Dube should choose Plan B and, before expanding further, guard the equipment, improve induction and reduce hours. He can review Plan A when profit has recovered.

parts.explanation: Weighs return against risk with the case evidence and recommends Plan B with conditions.
hints: Compare return and worst case, then add the evidence on profit and management.

explanation: Turnover 15.0%; wage bill up US\$72,000; net expected values US\$105,500 and US\$99,900; a cautious recommendation fixing the staff problems first.
hints: Labour turnover uses the average number of employees.
Net expected value = expected value − cost of the plan.
